cards.proposition: A lease deed that is inadmissible for non-registration renders all its terms, including clauses granting permission to sub-let, inadmissible in evidence; a tenant cannot rely on such unregistered terms to validate a sub-lease or claim exemption from eviction under Section 14(1) Proviso (b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. (Source: Court Interpretation of Registration Act principles applied to Lease Deed admissibility.)
cards.scope: Admissibility of lease terms regarding sub-letting when the primary lease document is unregistered and inadmissible for want of registration under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908. (Scope: Entire lease document and its specific clauses.)

conditions.text: The lease deed creating the tenancy is not registered under the Registration Act, 1908, making it inadmissible in evidence for proving the existence of the lease or its terms. (Kind: NECESSARY, Polarity: NEGATIVE, Factual Predicate: LEASE, Evidence: [p0004.s001], [p0004.s004], [p0005.s001], [p0005.s002])

evidence.quote: 4. The eviction proceeding was defended by the appellant on the ground that the M/s. United Automobiles are the authorised dealer and distributor of the product manufac- tured by the appellant and has been in occupation of the premises in that capacity and can not, therefore, be described as a sub-tenant. It was alternatively argued that in view of the term of the lease as quoted above the arrange- ment with the M/s. United Automobiles can not be condemned as a sublease without the consent of the respondent. The stand of the respondent has been that the above-mentioned term, of the lease can not be looked into as document was not registered and further the M/s.

In reply of the respondent's contention that the term can not be taken into consideration as the deed is not a regis- tered one, it was urged that the appellant, in view of the provisions of S. 49 of the Registration Act, is entitled to rely upon the term for 'collateral purpose'. The argument is that the document may not be admissible for the purpose of proving the existence of a lease or the terms thereof, but as the afore-mentioned clause does not come within that category, in as much as, it merely amounts to a written permission to the appellant to create a sub-lease, it can not be excluded from consideration on the ground of non- registration. 6.

registration, none of the terms of the lease can be admitted in evidence and that to use a document for the purpose of proving an important clause in the lease is not using it as a collateral purpose. 8. The learned counsel for the appellant attempted to meet the point by saying that so far the consent of the landlord permitting sub-letting is concerned, it does not require registration and the clause, therefore, must be excepted from the requirement of registration and consequent exclusion from evidence. We do not see any force in this argument.

The question whether a lessee is entitled to create a sub-lease, or not is undoubtedly a term of the transaction of lease, and if it is incorporated in the document it can not be disassociated from the lease and considered separately in isolation. If a document is inad- missible for non-registration, all its terms are inadmissi- ble including the one dealing with landlord's permission to his tenant to sub-let. It follows that the appellant can not, in the present circumstances, be allowed to rely upon the clause in his unregistered lease deed. 9. There is still another reason to hold that the afore- said clause can not come to the aid of the appellant.

cards.effect: The tenant is legally barred from relying on any clause within the unregistered deed that purports to grant consent for sub-letting, thereby failing to establish a defense against eviction on the ground of sub-letting. (Effect: Inability to validate sub-lease; Inability to claim consent exemption.)
formalization_limits: This rule applies strictly to the admissibility of the document itself; it does not validate the factual existence of the sub-lease relationship if the document is inadmissible, but rather prevents the tenant from using the document to prove the landlord's consent. (Limit: Distinction between factual occurrence and evidentiary proof of consent.)

The rule does not address whether the sub-lease was factually created, only that the written consent clause cannot be used as legal justification due to the inadmissibility of the source document. (Limit: Scope restricted to evidentiary admissibility of consent clause.)
